questions.q: Zoya is the 5th girl in a line of children, all of different heights, and she calls 2 by the heights rule. Which statement must be true?
questions.a: Of the 4 children in front of her, 2 are taller and 2 are shorter. The call counts only taller children in front, so it says nothing about which two they are, and nothing about the children behind her.
o: Of the 4 children in front of her, 2 are taller and 2 are shorter.
The 2 children standing right in front of her are the taller ones.
She is the 3rd tallest child in the whole line.
Two of the children behind her are taller than she is.

questions.q: Six children stand in this order from the front, with heights 4, 1, 3, 6, 2, 5 (6 is the tallest). If every child calls the number of taller children in front of her, the total of all six calls is ___.
In a line of 8 children, no two of the same height, exactly three children call 0. Which statement must be true?
questions.a: The tallest child of the line is the last of the three who called 0. A child standing behind the tallest child has her in front and so cannot call 0, while the tallest herself calls 0. The first 0-caller need not be the tallest, and the shortest child need not be a 0-caller.
o: The tallest child of the line is the last of the three who called 0.
The tallest child of the line is the first of the three who called 0.
The shortest child of the line is one of the three who called 0.
The three children who called 0 stand at places 1, 2 and 3.

questions.q: In a queue of children of different heights, Imran is 5th and calls 4. Joy stands right behind him, 6th, and calls 0. Which statement must be true?
questions.a: Imran is the shortest of the six and Joy is the tallest of the six. Imran calls 4, so he is shorter than the four ahead of him. Joy calls 0, so she is taller than all five in front, Imran included.
o: Imran is the shortest of the six children and Joy is the tallest of the six.
Imran is the shortest of the six children, but Joy may not be the tallest of the six.
Joy is the tallest of the six children, but Imran may be taller than one of the first four.
Joy is shorter than Imran, because the 6th child has more children in front of her.

questions.q: Nine children line up for the annual day photograph, no two of the same height. The 3rd child calls 0 and the 7th child calls 0. Which statement must be true?
questions.a: The 7th child calls 0, so she is taller than all six in front, including the 3rd child. The 8th or 9th child could still be taller than her.
o: The 7th child is taller than the 3rd child.
The 3rd child is taller than the 7th child.
The 3rd and 7th children are of the same height.
The 7th child is the tallest of all nine children.

questions.q:
Read these statements about the heights game (all children are of different heights).
Statement 1: A child who calls 3 must be standing 3rd in the line.
Statement 2: A child who calls 3 stands 4th or later in the line.
Statement 3: If the last child in a line calls 0, she is the tallest in the line.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: a child needs three children in front to call 3, so she is 4th or later, not 3rd.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If all seven children in a line call 0, they stand in order of increasing height from the front to the back.
Reason (R): The first child in any line calls 0.
questions.a: Both are true but R does not explain A. Each child calling 0 means each is taller than everyone in front, which forces increasing heights. The first child calling 0 is true of every line and says nothing about the others.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each list of calls for five children (all of different heights) with what it says about the line.
1. 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
2. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
3. 0, 1, 1, 1, 1
4. 0, 0, 0, 3, 3
(a) Heights fall steadily from the front to the back.
(b) Heights rise steadily from the front to the back.
(c) The first child is the tallest; the other four rise in height.
(d) The first three rise in height; the last two are shorter than all of them, the fifth taller than the fourth.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. All zeros mean each child is taller than everyone in front (rising). 0 to 4 means each is shorter than all in front (falling). 0, 1, 1, 1, 1 means only the first child is taller than any later child. 0, 0, 0, 3, 3 means the last two are below the first three.

questions.q: Five children of heights 3, 5, 2, 4 and 1 units (5 is the tallest) stand in this order from the front. (a) Write the number each child calls. (b) Which child calls the largest number, and why must she call it?
questions.a: (a) 0, 0, 2, 1, 4. (b) The last child (height 1): she is the shortest, so all four children in front of her are taller.
s: Part (a): writes the calls 0, 0, 2, 1, 4 by counting taller children in front
Part (b): names the last child as the shortest, so all four in front are taller

questions.q: Five children, all of different heights, call 0, 1, 1, 0, 4 in that order. (a) Which child (1st to 5th) is the tallest and which is the shortest? (b) Write their heights as 1 (shortest) to 5 (tallest), in the order they stand.
questions.a: (a) The 4th child is the tallest (she calls 0 and the 5th child has four taller in front); the 5th is the shortest (4 taller in front). (b) 4, 2, 3, 5, 1.
s: Part (a): 4th child tallest, 5th child shortest, with the reason from the calls
Part (b): arranges the heights as 4, 2, 3, 5, 1

questions.q: Four children of different heights stand in a line. (a) List every number the 4th child could possibly call. (b) A fifth child, taller than all four, now joins at the back of the line. What does she call, and do the four earlier calls change? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 0, 1, 2 or 3 (at most three children are in front of her). (b) She calls 0, because nobody in front is taller. The earlier calls do not change, because each child counts only the children in front, and the new child is behind them.
s: Part (a): lists 0, 1, 2, 3
Part (b): she calls 0 and the earlier calls stay the same, with the in-front reason

questions.q: Three children of heights 150 cm, 160 cm and 155 cm stand in this order. Aman, whose height is a whole number of cm between 152 and 158 and different from every other child's, joins at the back as the 4th child. (a) List every number he could call. (b) Aman's friend Bela is 148 cm and joins the back of the same line behind Aman. What does she call, and does it depend on Aman's exact height?
questions.a: (a) Aman calls 1 or 2: heights 153 or 154 have 160 and 155 taller (2); heights 156 or 157 have only 160 taller (1). (b) Bela calls 4: all of 150, 160, 155 and Aman are taller than 148, whatever Aman's exact height is.
s: Part (a): finds the calls 1 and 2 by splitting Aman's height at 155 cm
Part (b): Bela calls 4 and the call does not depend on Aman's height

questions.q: Four children of different heights stand with calls 0, 0, 2, 1 in order. (a) A new child, taller than all four, steps in at the front of the line. Write the five calls now. (b) If the new child were shorter than all four, which calls would change? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 0, 1, 1, 3, 2: the new child calls 0 and each of the four old children gains one taller child in front. (b) None of the old calls change, because the new shortest child is not taller than anyone; she calls 0 and the line reads 0, 0, 0, 2, 1.
s: Part (a): writes 0, 1, 1, 3, 2 with the reason that every old call rises by 1
Part (b): no old call changes because she is shorter than everyone; the line is 0, 0, 0, 2, 1

questions.q: Farhan says: 'In a line of 6 children of different heights, if one child calls 5, she must be the last child and the shortest child of all.' Do you agree? Explain with the rule of the game.
questions.a: Yes, Farhan is right. Calling 5 needs five taller children in front of her, so at least five children stand in front and she is the 6th, the last. All five in front are taller than her and she is behind no one else, so she is the shortest of the six.
s: Gives the verdict that Farhan is right
Reasons that 5 taller children in front puts her 6th
Concludes all other five are taller, so she is shortest

questions.q: A teacher records the calls 0, 1, 0, 4, 2, 5 for six children standing in a line, all of different heights. Show that these calls cannot be correct, and state the rule that every list of calls must obey.
questions.a: The 4th child calls 4, but only 3 children stand in front of her, so at most 3 can be taller. Rule: the child in place k from the front can call at most k - 1 (the 1st child calls 0, the 2nd at most 1, and so on).
s: Spots that the 4th child calls 4 with only 3 children in front
Explains that she can count at most 3
States the rule: the child in place k calls at most k - 1

questions.q: Seven children of different heights call 0, 0, 2, 0, 4, 2, 5 in order. Giving the shortest child the height 1 and the tallest 7, find their heights in the order they stand. Show how you started.
questions.a: Start from the last child: she calls 5 with 6 in front, so exactly 5 are taller, which makes her the 2nd shortest of the seven (height 2). Remove her and repeat with the remaining six. Heights: 4, 6, 3, 7, 1, 5, 2.
s: Starts from the last child and links her call to her rank among all seven (height 2)
Repeats the idea on the remaining children, removing one at a time
Writes the full order 4, 6, 3, 7, 1, 5, 2

questions.q:
For each statement about children in a line (all of different heights), say whether it is always true, only sometimes true or never true, and give a reason or an example.
(i) If the 3rd child calls 2, both children in front of her are taller than she is.
(ii) Two children in the same line call the same number.
(iii) In a line of 9 children, one child calls 9.
(iv) The last child's call equals the number of children in the line who are taller than she is.
(v) The child who calls the largest number is the last child in the line.
questions.a: (i) Always: she has only two children in front and 2 of them are taller. (ii) Only sometimes: calls 0, 1, 1 repeat a number, but 0, 1, 2 do not. (iii) Never: at most 8 children are in front of any child. (iv) Always: every other child is in front of the last child, so all taller children are counted. (v) Only sometimes: heights 3, 4, 2, 1, 5 give 0, 0, 2, 3, 0, where the 4th child calls the largest number and the last child calls 0.
s: (i) Always true with reason
(ii) Only sometimes true with two example lines
(iii) Never true because at most 8 children are in front
(iv) Always true because everyone else is in front of the last child
(v) Only sometimes true with a counter-example line

questions.q:
Five children of heights 2, 5, 1, 4, 3 stand in a line. Then the line is reversed, so the order becomes 3, 4, 1, 5, 2.
(a) Write the calls for the first line.
(b) Write the calls for the reversed line.
(c) Find the total of the calls in each line.
(d) Add the two totals and compare the sum with 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.
(e) For three children of heights 2, 1, 3 and their reverse, find the combined total of the calls. Use the pattern in (d) and (e) to predict the combined total for a line of 8 children and its reverse, and check it using heights 1 to 8 in order.
questions.a: (a) 0, 0, 2, 1, 2. (b) 0, 0, 2, 0, 3. (c) 5 and 5. (d) 10, which equals 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. (e) Heights 2, 1, 3 call 0, 1, 0 (total 1) and the reverse 3, 1, 2 calls 0, 1, 1 (total 2), so 3 = 1 + 2. For 8 children the pattern gives 1 + 2 + ... + 7 = 28. Check: heights 1 to 8 in order call all 0 (total 0), the reverse calls 0, 1, ..., 7 (total 28), so the combined total is 28.
s: Part (a): calls 0, 0, 2, 1, 2
Part (b): calls 0, 0, 2, 0, 3
Part (c): totals 5 and 5
Part (d): sum 10 equals 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
Part (e): total 3 for three children, predicts 28 and checks with heights 1 to 8

questions.q:
For the sports day march-past, Mr Qureshi lines up six children in this order: Aarav (142 cm), Bela (149 cm), Charu (138 cm), Dev (151 cm), Esha (135 cm) and Farid (146 cm). Each child calls the number of taller children in front of her or him. A child with three or more taller children in front cannot see the stage. He is considering three plans: keep this order, line up shortest first, or line up tallest first. The school banner must be carried by the three tallest children, who have to walk in the first three places.
(a) Write the six numbers the children call in the present order.
(b) Which children call 0, and who among them is the tallest child of all?
(c) For each of the three plans, how many children cannot see the stage?
(d) Which plan should he choose? Weigh the counts from (c) against the banner rule.
questions.a: (a) 0, 0, 2, 0, 4, 2. (b) Aarav, Bela and Dev call 0; Dev (151 cm) is the tallest of all, while Aarav and Bela only have nobody taller in front of them. (c) Present order: 1 child (Esha, who calls 4). Shortest first: 0 children (all call 0). Tallest first: calls 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 so 3 children cannot see. (d) Shortest first lets every child see the stage (0 cannot see) but breaks the banner rule, since the three tallest children walk last. Tallest first obeys the banner rule but 3 children cannot see; keeping the present order has 1 child who cannot see and also breaks the banner rule. A sound choice is shortest first if seeing the stage comes first, or tallest first if the banner rule is compulsory, stating the cost of 3 children who cannot see.
s: Part (a): calls 0, 0, 2, 0, 4, 2
Part (b): names Aarav, Bela, Dev and picks Dev as tallest
Part (c): counts 1, 0 and 3 children who cannot see
Part (d): chooses a plan and justifies it by weighing the counts against the banner rule

questions.q:
Seven students of Class 7B stand in a line for a photograph. Ms Kaur does not know their heights, but each student calls a number by the heights rule (no two students have the same height). The calls, in order from the left, are 0, 1, 1, 0, 4, 1, 6. The back row of the photograph has room for exactly 4 students, and the three shortest sit in the front row.
(a) Which student (1st to 7th) is the tallest and which is the shortest?
(b) Write the heights as 1 (shortest) to 7 (tallest) for the seven students, in the order they stand.
(c) Which students, by their place in the line, sit in the front row?
(d) The photographer suggests: 'Put every student who called 0 or 1 in the back row.' Will that suit the back row? Give your reason.
questions.a: (a) The tallest must call 0, so she is the 1st or the 4th student; the 4th calls 0 and so is taller than the 1st, which makes the 4th the tallest. The 7th is the shortest (all 6 in front are taller). (b) 5, 3, 4, 7, 2, 6, 1. (c) The three shortest have heights 1, 2, 3, which are the 7th, 5th and 2nd students. (d) No. Students who called 0 or 1 are the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th: five students, more than the 4 places, and the 2nd student (height 3) is one of the front-row students. A call only compares a student with those in front, so it does not rank her in the whole line.
s: Part (a): 4th tallest, 7th shortest with reasons from the calls
Part (b): heights 5, 3, 4, 7, 2, 6, 1
Part (c): front row is the 2nd, 5th and 7th students
Part (d): rejects the suggestion: five students qualify and the 2nd belongs in front

questions.q: Five consecutive whole numbers add up to 2,015. Without finding them, what must be true of the smallest and the largest of the five?
questions.a: Both are odd. If the smallest is odd, the five numbers run odd, even, odd, even, odd: three odd addends, so the sum is odd. If the smallest is even, there are only two odd addends and the sum is even. 2,015 is odd, so the smallest is odd, and the largest (four more) is odd too.
o: The smallest and the largest are both odd.
The smallest and the largest are both even.
The smallest is odd and the largest is even.
Nothing about their parity can be said without finding them.

questions.q: True or False: Rahul adds 9 odd numbers and 4 even numbers, and then adds one more odd number. The final sum is an even number.
questions.a: True. 9 odd numbers (an odd count) add to an odd number, and 4 even numbers add to an even number, so the first sum is odd + even = odd. Adding one more odd number gives odd + odd = even.
s: Gives the verdict True
Reasons: odd count of odd numbers is odd, then odd + odd is even

questions.q: Sana and her cousin Ritu were born exactly one year apart. On Sana's birthday the sum of their ages is 77. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Ages one year apart are consecutive numbers, one even and one odd, so their sum is odd; 77 is odd and 38 + 39 = 77. 37 and 40 add to 77 but are three years apart.
o: It is possible: their ages are 38 and 39.
It is impossible: the sum of two consecutive numbers is always even.
It is impossible: 77 is odd, but ages must add up to an even number.
It is possible: their ages are 37 and 40.

questions.q:
At the school fair, a tuck shop sells samosas at ₹15, juice at ₹20, rolls at ₹35 and tea at ₹10. At closing time: 17 samosas, 24 juices, 13 rolls and 6 teas were sold. Three helpers report the day's takings: Gaurav says ₹1,247, Hina says ₹1,250 and Imran says ₹1,258. The principal can either check only the parity of each report, which takes seconds, or add up all the sales, which takes much longer.
(a) Without multiplying, say whether the takings from each item (samosa, juice, roll, tea) are odd or even.
(b) What is the parity of the total takings?
(c) Which of the three reports does the quick parity check reject?
(d) Which reports still need the long addition? What would you advise the principal to do?
questions.a: (a) Samosas 17 x 15 odd; juice 24 x 20 even; rolls 13 x 35 odd; tea 6 x 10 even. (b) odd + even + odd + even = even. (c) Gaurav's ₹1,247 is odd, so it is rejected. (d) Hina's 1,250 and Imran's 1,258 are both even, so parity cannot choose between them; the long addition (255 + 480 + 455 + 60 = 1,250) shows Hina is right and Imran is wrong. Advice: use parity first to throw out reports that fail, then add up only for the rest.
s: Part (a): parities odd, even, odd, even for the four items
Part (b): total is even
Part (c): rejects Gaurav's ₹1,247
Part (d): says the even reports need real addition, giving Hina's 1,250, and advises parity first then addition

questions.q: Two whole numbers add up to 41. (a) Can their difference be 7? Can it be 8? Decide each without trying every pair. (b) Explain why a sum and a difference of the same two numbers always have the same parity.
questions.a: (a) 7 is possible (24 + 17 = 41 and 24 - 17 = 7); 8 is impossible, because 41 is odd, so one number is even and one is odd, and their difference must be odd. (b) The sum and the difference differ by twice the smaller number, which is even, and two numbers that differ by an even number have the same parity.
s: Part (a): 7 possible with 24 and 17, 8 impossible because an odd sum forces an odd difference
Part (b): sum and difference differ by an even amount, so the parities match

questions.q: Radha's piggy bank has an odd number of ₹1 coins, an odd number of ₹5 coins and some ₹20 coins. She says the total is ₹487. Show, using parity, that she cannot be right.
questions.a: An odd number of ₹1 coins is worth an odd amount. An odd number of ₹5 coins is also worth an odd amount (5 x odd = odd). ₹20 coins are worth an even amount. odd + odd + even = even, but 487 is odd, so the total cannot be ₹487.
s: Finds the parity of the ₹1 and ₹5 coin values (both odd)
Finds the ₹20 coins give an even amount and adds the parities: even
Concludes 487 is odd so it is impossible

questions.q:
Zubin has seven cards numbered 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13. He puts exactly one card in each box of a row of boxes and adds the numbers.
(a) With 6 boxes, find the six cards that total 40.
(b) With 5 boxes, can the total be 36? Explain.
(c) With 3 boxes, find three cards that total 29.
(d) He wants a total of 28. Which numbers of boxes could give it? Use parity first, then size, to rule out the rest.
questions.a: (a) The cards add to 49; leave out 9 to get 40: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 11 + 13. (b) No: five odd numbers always add to an odd number, and 36 is even. (c) 5 + 11 + 13 = 29. (d) Parity allows only 2, 4 or 6 boxes. Two cards give at most 13 + 11 = 24, which is below 28. Six cards give 49 minus the left-out card, so 28 needs 21 to be left out, and there is no such card. Four cards can work, for example 1 + 3 + 11 + 13 = 28. So only 4 boxes.
s: Part (a): six cards totalling 40 (all but 9)
Part (b): no, five odd numbers give an odd total
Part (c): a valid set of three cards totalling 29
Part (d): parity leaves 2, 4 or 6 boxes; size removes 2 and 6; 4 works with an example

questions.q:
(a) Find the parity of 19 x 23 x 51 without multiplying.
(b) Find the parity of 38 x 15 x 27 without multiplying.
(c) Six numbers are multiplied and the product is odd. What do you know about each of the six numbers?
(d) Can two numbers have an odd product and an odd sum? Give a reason.
(e) Show that a x b x (a + b) is even whenever a and b are whole numbers.
questions.a: (a) Odd (every factor is odd). (b) Even (38 is even). (c) All six are odd. (d) No: an odd product needs both numbers odd, and the sum of two odd numbers is even. (e) If a or b is even, the product ab is even. If both are odd, a + b is even, so the whole product is even. Either way it is even.
s: Part (a): odd, as all factors are odd
Part (b): even, because of the factor 38
Part (c): every one of the six is odd
Part (d): never, as an odd product forces two odd numbers whose sum is even
Part (e): checks both cases (one even, or both odd) and finds the product even

questions.q: Anu draws 8 cards showing odd numbers and 5 cards showing even numbers. She says the sum of all 13 cards is 150. A friend says parity alone can test the claim. What does the parity check show?
questions.a: The total must be even, so 150 is not ruled out by parity. 8 odd numbers add to an even number and 5 even numbers add to an even number. Parity can reject a claim, but an even claim passing the check is not proved right.
o: The total must be even, so 150 is not ruled out by parity.
The total must be odd, because 13 cards is an odd count.
The total must be odd, because odd and even numbers are mixed.
The total must be even, so 150 is certainly the correct total.

questions.q: Three Class 7 sections have 23, 19 and 27 students. In a pairing game each section pairs off within itself, and a student without a partner sits out. (a) How many students sit out in each section? (b) If the leftover students from different sections are allowed to pair with one another, can all 69 students end up in pairs? Give the parity reason.
questions.a: (a) One student sits out in each section (each number is odd), so 3 in all. (b) No: the three leftovers can make only one pair, and one student remains. The reason is that the total 23 + 19 + 27 = 69 is a sum of three odd numbers, which is odd.
s: Part (a): one student sits out in each of the three sections
Part (b): no, 69 is odd (three odd numbers add to an odd number), so one is left over

questions.q: a and b are whole numbers. Kabir tries a few pairs and finds that a x b + a + b is odd. What can he safely say about a and b?
questions.a: At least one of a and b is odd. If both are even, ab, a and b are all even and the sum is even. If exactly one is odd, ab and the even number are even and the odd one makes the total odd. If both are odd, ab, a and b are all odd and three odds add to an odd number.
o: At least one of a and b is odd.
Both a and b are odd.
Exactly one of a and b is odd.
a and b are both even.

questions.q: Twenty whole numbers are added and the total is odd. Which of these could be the number of odd numbers among the twenty?
questions.a: 9. The total is odd only when the count of odd addends is odd, and 9 is the only odd count offered; 6, 14 and 20 are even counts and give even totals.

questions.q: (a) Without calculating, find the parity of 35 x 22 + 17 x 19 + 48 x 50. (b) Rubina changes the 22 to 23. Does the parity of the whole expression change? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) 35 x 22 is even, 17 x 19 is odd and 48 x 50 is even, so even + odd + even = odd (the value is 3,493). (b) Yes: 35 x 23 is now odd, so odd + odd + even = even (the value is 3,528).
s: Part (a): parities even, odd, even and total odd
Part (b): the first product turns odd, so the total becomes even and the parity changes

questions.q:
Read these statements about parity.
Statement 1: The sum of any 5 odd numbers is odd.
Statement 2: The difference of two odd numbers is odd.
Statement 3: The product of an odd number and an even number is even.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: odd - odd = even (for example 15 - 9 = 6).
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Write the totals 1 + 2, 1 + 2 + 3, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, and so on up to 1 + 2 + ... + 10. The number of odd totals among these nine is ___.

A lamp is ON. Meera toggles its switch 15 times, Neel 22 times and Omar 9 times. (a) Is the lamp ON or OFF at the end? (b) Four children together toggle the switch 100 times and three of them toggled an odd number of times each. Is the fourth child's count odd or even, and why?
questions.a: (a) ON: 15 + 22 + 9 = 46 is even, and an even number of toggles brings the lamp back to ON. (b) Odd: three odd counts add to an odd number, and the total 100 is even, so the fourth count must be odd (odd + odd = even).
s: Part (a): total toggles 46 is even, so the lamp is ON
Part (b): three odd counts sum to odd, so the fourth must be odd to reach 100

questions.q: Find the parity of the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 75 without adding them one by one. Then check your answer by finding the actual sum (the sum of the numbers from 1 to 75 is 75 x 76 / 2).
questions.a: Among 1 to 75 there are 38 odd numbers (1, 3, ..., 75). Thirty-eight is an even count of odd numbers, so their sum is even; the even numbers add an even sum. The total is even. Check: 75 x 76 / 2 = 2850, which is even.
s: Counts the odd numbers from 1 to 75 as 38
Argues even count of odd numbers gives an even sum, so the whole sum is even
Checks with 2850 being even

questions.q: Sana says: 'The sum of three whole numbers can be odd only when at least one of the three numbers is odd.' Do you agree? Then say whether having one odd number among the three is enough to make the sum odd, using an example.
questions.a: Yes, she is right: three even numbers always add to an even number, so an odd sum needs at least one odd addend. But one odd number is not enough: 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 has odd addends and an even sum. The sum is odd exactly when the count of odd addends is odd (1 or 3).
s: Agrees, because three even numbers give an even sum
Shows one odd addend is not enough with an example such as 3 + 5 + 4 = 12
States the sum is odd exactly when the count of odd addends is odd

questions.q:
The Annual Day hall at Navjyoti School has three seating blocks. Block P has 23 rows of 18 seats, Block Q has 19 rows of 25 seats and Block R has 28 rows of 15 seats. Students will sit in pairs for a buddy activity, and each block is seated separately, so every block must have an even number of seats. The principal can add one more row to exactly one block: a row in P has 18 seats, in Q has 25 seats and in R has 15 seats.
(a) Without multiplying, find whether each block has an odd or an even number of seats.
(b) Find the total number of seats in the hall. Is it odd or even?
(c) The brochure says the hall has 1,310 seats. Use parity to say whether that can be right.
(d) Which block should get the extra row so that every block can be filled by pairs? Show why each of the other two blocks fails.
questions.a: (a) P: 23 x 18 even (18 is even); Q: 19 x 25 odd; R: 28 x 15 even. (b) 414 + 475 + 420 = 1,309, which is odd. (c) No: even + odd + even is odd, so the total cannot be 1,310. (d) Only Q works. Q has 475 seats (odd) and the extra row of 25 (odd) makes it 500, even; P (414) and R (420) are already even. Adding Q's row is the only way to turn the one odd block even. Adding to P (18, even) leaves Q odd; adding to R (15, odd) makes R 435, odd, and Q stays odd too. The hall total after Q's row is 1,334, also even.
s: Part (a): P even, Q odd, R even using parity of factors
Part (b): total 1,309, odd
Part (c): says 1,310 is impossible because the total is odd
Part (d): chooses Q and shows P and R fail because Q stays odd (and R turns odd)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The number of small squares in a 27 x 13 grid is odd.

questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: 27 and 13 are both odd, so 27 x 13 (= 351) is odd.

questions.q:
In a street in Pune the houses on the left are numbered 1, 3, 5, ... and the houses on the right are numbered 2, 4, 6, ... so that the n-th house on the left faces the n-th house on the right.
(a) Which house faces number 99?
(b) Write the sum of the numbers of any two facing houses in terms of n.
(c) Is this sum odd or even? Explain.
(d) Can two facing houses have numbers adding to 250? Why or why not?
(e) Which two facing houses have numbers adding to 251?
questions.a: (a) 99 = 2n - 1 gives n = 50, so house 100 faces it. (b) (2n - 1) + 2n = 4n - 1. (c) Odd: 4n is even and subtracting 1 makes it odd. (d) No, 250 is even. (e) 4n - 1 = 251 gives n = 63: houses 125 and 126.
s: Part (a): finds house 100 using n = 50
Part (b): writes 4n - 1
Part (c): says odd with a reason
Part (d): says no because 250 is even
Part (e): n = 63, houses 125 and 126

questions.q:
Read these statements about expressions (the letters stand for whole numbers).

Statement 2: The expression 3p + 3 gives odd numbers for some values of p and even numbers for others.
Statement 3: Every even number can be written as 8j - 6 for some whole number j.

questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: 8j - 6 gives 2, 10, 18, ... and misses even numbers such as 4 and 6.

questions.q: Ishaan numbers the n-th packet of a batch with a rule and wants every packet number to be even, whatever the whole number n is. Which rule works?
questions.a: n(n + 1). It is the product of two consecutive numbers, one of which is even, so the product is even for every n. n(n + 2) is odd for odd n, n + (n + 1) is always odd, and 3n + 4 alternates.

questions.q: The expressions 2p + 1 (p = 0, 1, 2, ...) and 2q - 1 (q = 1, 2, 3, ...) both list the odd numbers. (a) Find the value of p and the value of q that give the odd number 41. (b) Explain how the two expressions are connected, and why the same value of the letter-number gives different odd numbers.
questions.a: (a) 2p + 1 = 41 gives p = 20, and 2q - 1 = 41 gives q = 21. (b) 2q - 1 = 2(q - 1) + 1, so q is always one more than p for the same odd number: the lists are the same, only the counting starts differently (p from 0, q from 1), so p = 3 and q = 3 give 7 and 5.
s: Part (a): p = 20 and q = 21
Part (b): q = p + 1 for the same number, as the two lists start counting at 0 and at 1, so equal values of the letter give different odd numbers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The n-th odd number is 2n - 1.
Reason (R): The number 2n is even for every whole number n.
questions.a: Both are true but R does not explain A. R only says that 2n is even. The reason the n-th odd number is 2n - 1 is that each odd number is one less than the even number at the same position.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Part (b): odd n gives even value, with the parity reason

questions.q: The tickets of a school raffle are numbered 3, 7, 11, 15, ... in the order they are sold. Write an expression for the number on the n-th ticket, find the number on the 30th ticket, and say whether any ticket can have an even number.
questions.a: Each ticket number is 4 times the position less 1: 4n - 1 (n = 1 gives 3, n = 2 gives 7). The 30th ticket is 4 x 30 - 1 = 119. 4n is even, so 4n - 1 is always odd and no ticket has an even number.

Finds the 30th ticket as 119

questions.q: Tarun says: 'The expression 7n + 5 has the same parity as n: it is even when n is even and odd when n is odd.' Do you agree? Support your answer with one value of n of each kind.
questions.a: No, he is wrong; the parity is the opposite of n's. When n is odd, 7n is odd and odd + 5 (odd) is even: n = 3 gives 26. When n is even, 7n is even and even + 5 is odd: n = 4 gives 33. So 7n + 5 is even for odd n and odd for even n.
s: Disagrees with Tarun, with the odd n case reasoned (n = 3 gives 26, even)
Reasons the even n case (7n even, plus 5 is odd)
Checks with n = 4 giving 33 and states the parity is opposite to n's

questions.q: (a) For which value of n does 3n + 4 equal 100? (b) Show that 12m + 7 can never equal 300, whatever whole number m is.
questions.a: (a) 3n = 96 gives n = 32. (b) 12m is a multiple of 2, so it is even; adding 7 gives an odd number every time. 300 is even, so 12m + 7 can never be 300.

Part (b): 12m is even so 12m + 7 is odd

Part (b): solves 2n - 1 = 91 to get the 46th

questions.q: Radha adds the expressions 5n and 3n and then adds 7 to get 5n + 3n + 7, where n is a whole number. What can she say about the parity of the result?
questions.a: It is always odd. 5n + 3n = 8n, which is even for every n, and an even number plus 7 is odd. (When n is odd, 5n and 3n are both odd and add to an even number, so the result is still odd.)
o: Always odd, as 5n + 3n is always even.
Odd for odd n and even for even n.

questions.q: Ritu adds three consecutive whole numbers starting from n, that is n + (n + 1) + (n + 2). Which statement about the sum is correct?
questions.a: The sum is even when n is odd and odd when n is even. The sum is 3n + 3: n = 1 gives 6 and n = 2 gives 9. Its parity follows the parity of n + 1, so it alternates.

questions.q: (a) Find the value of 3n + 4 for n = 5 and for n = 6 and write the parity of each. (b) As n goes up by 1 each time, does the parity of 3n + 4 alternate? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) n = 5 gives 19 (odd); n = 6 gives 22 (even). (b) Yes: 3n changes between odd and even each time n goes up by 1 (3 x odd is odd, 3 x even is even), and adding 4 does not change parity.
s: Part (a): 19 odd and 22 even
Part (b): says yes with the reason that 3n alternates and +4 keeps parity

questions.q:
Say whether each statement is true or false (n and the other letters stand for whole numbers) and give a reason or a counter-example.
(i) The expression 8m + 6 always gives an even number.
(ii) The expression 5s - 2 always gives an odd number.
(iii) The expression 2t + 9 always gives an odd number.
(iv) Every odd number can be written as 4u + 1.
(v) The expression 7n + 7 gives an even number whenever n is odd.
questions.a: (i) True: 8m is even and 6 is even. (ii) False: s = 2 gives 8, which is even. (iii) True: 2t is even and adding 9 gives an odd number. (iv) False: 3 and 7 cannot be written as 4u + 1. (v) True: 7n + 7 = 7(n + 1) and n + 1 is even when n is odd.
s: (i) true with reason
(ii) false with a counter-example
(iii) true with reason
(iv) false with an odd number that cannot be 4u + 1
(v) true with reason

questions.q:
Sonal's stationery shop in Nagpur numbers the n-th bill of each day by a rule. Her father wants every bill number even so carbon copies can be filed in pairs, and he also wants consecutive bill numbers at least 4 apart so that rivals cannot count the day's bills. The bill book is printed with the numbers 1 to 250 only. A normal day has 50 bills but a festival day has about 70. She is choosing among the rules 3n + 4, 4n + 2 and 2n + 30.
(a) Find the first three bill numbers under each rule. Which rule fails the 'always even' test, and which numbers show it?
(b) Explain, using parity, why the other two rules always give even numbers.
(c) What is the largest number of bills a day that each of 4n + 2 and 2n + 30 can serve before the book runs out?
(d) Which rule should Sonal choose? Weigh the 4-apart wish against the festival day.
questions.a: (a) 3n + 4: 7, 10, 13; 4n + 2: 6, 10, 14; 2n + 30: 32, 34, 36. The rule 3n + 4 fails, because 7 and 13 are odd. (b) 4n and 2n are even for every n, and adding the even numbers 2 and 30 keeps them even. (c) 4n + 2 <= 250 gives n <= 62, so 62 bills; 2n + 30 <= 250 gives n <= 110, so 110 bills. (d) 4n + 2 meets the 4-apart wish and serves a normal day (50 bills, last number 202), but on a festival day of 70 bills it runs out after the 62nd, so she needs a second book then. 2n + 30 serves even a festival day (the 70th bill is 170) but its numbers are only 2 apart, which breaks the father's wish. A sound choice is 4n + 2 with a spare book for festival days, or 2n + 30 if filing alone matters; the reasoning must use both counts.
s: Part (a): lists 7, 10, 13 / 6, 10, 14 / 32, 34, 36 and rejects 3n + 4
Part (b): 4n and 2n are even and the added 2 and 30 are even
Part (c): 62 bills for 4n + 2 and 110 bills for 2n + 30
Part (d): chooses a rule and weighs the 4-apart wish against the 70-bill festival day using the counts

questions.q: A shopkeeper tags shelves 3, 9, 15, 21, ... in order. (a) Write an expression for the tag on the n-th shelf and say whether any tag can be even. (b) Which shelf carries the tag 105?
questions.a: (a) The tags go up by 6 starting from 3, so the n-th tag is 6n - 3 (n = 1 gives 3, n = 2 gives 9). 6n is even and taking away 3 leaves an odd number, so no tag is even. (b) 6n - 3 = 105 gives n = 18, the 18th shelf.
s: Part (a): writes 6n - 3 and says every tag is odd because 6n is even
Part (b): solves 6n - 3 = 105 to get the 18th shelf

questions.a: It is impossible. The sum is (2n - 1) + (2n + 1) = 4n, which is a multiple of 4, and 90 is not a multiple of 4 (4n = 90 would need n = 22.5).

questions.q:
At a temple in Madurai, two counters give out prasadam tokens in the order devotees arrive. Counter A gives out tokens 1, 3, 5, 7, ... and Counter B gives out tokens 2, 4, 6, 8, ... Each counter has printed tokens only up to 200. On a festival day 210 devotees are expected. The trust can either reprint the tokens at both counters to go up to 220, or open a third counter for the last 10 devotees.
(a) What token number does the 60th devotee at Counter A get, and the 60th at Counter B?
(b) Which devotee at Counter A gets token 157?
(c) How many devotees can each counter serve with tokens up to 200?
(d) Which option would you recommend for the 210 devotees, and why?
questions.a: (a) A: 2 x 60 - 1 = 119; B: 2 x 60 = 120. (b) 2n - 1 = 157 gives n = 79, the 79th devotee. (c) 100 each (tokens 1 to 199 and 2 to 200), so 200 in all, which is 10 short of 210. (d) Reprinting up to 220 lets A serve 110 and B serve 110, a total of 220, enough for all 210 with no new counter. A third counter for 10 devotees also works, but needs extra staff for few people. Reprinting is simpler.
s: Part (a): 119 and 120
Part (b): the 79th devotee
Part (c): 100 each, 200 in all
Part (d): recommends an option and checks it covers 210 using the counts

Tara says: 'If a circled sum of a filled 3 x 3 grid of 1 to 9 is 8, the three numbers on that line must include 1.' Do you agree? Would the same be true for a circled sum of 9? Give the possible sets.

questions.a: (a) 9 + 1 + 2 = 12: the other two numbers in that row are at best the two smallest. (b) 2 + 8 + 9 = 19: the other two numbers are at best the two largest. So the row with 9 can never show a circle below 12, and the row with 2 can never show one above 19.

questions.q: A 3 x 3 grid is filled with the numbers 2 to 10, each used once. The three row circles of a solved grid must add up to ___.

At the school fair, the Maths club runs a 'Magic Mat' stall. Visitors fill a 3 x 3 mat with number tiles 1 to 9, each used once. Four clue cards are ready. Card A: rows 15, 8, 22; columns 9, 15, 21. Card B: rows 8, 14, 22; columns 13, 12, 20. Card C: rows 5, 18, 22; columns 9, 16, 20. Card D: rows 6, 16, 23; columns 6, 17, 22. The club will print only cards that have a solution. questions.q:

questions.a: (a) Third row: 45 - 14 - 20 = 11. Second column: 45 - 15 - 12 = 18. (b) For example 1 6 7 / 9 8 3 / 5 4 2: rows 14, 20, 11 and columns 15, 18, 12.
